However, after that interview, I tried to refresh my memory because it had been a long time ago. And together with my colleagues, I wanted to clarify to myself the position of the Crisis Staff and the Executive Board. In my first interview, I didn't have a clear picture because I'm not a lawyer by profession, and I was not familiar with the organisation of the state administration. That's why I tried to clarify these two things for myself. And I am sure that the Crisis Staff, according to the regulations and according to the enactment that regulated its work, could not stand in for the Executive Board. But I'm sure that some of the issues overlapped, that is, the issues that were discussed at the Crisis Staff which pertained to the area of responsibility of the members of the Executive Board who were also members of the Crisis Staff. This would be my explanation. I was one of those people who asked Dr. Kovacevic to abolish the Crisis Staff because I thought at that time, and that was later on confirmed, that this Crisis Staff as a matter of fact was not the body that had a decisive role in many of the things that encumbered the situation at that time. And however, it was blamed for a lot of things that were happening at the level of the municipality. And that was the only reason for which I asked Mr. Kovacevic to ask the president of the Crisis Staff to abolish that body because we, as a body, could not have any influence on the situation on the ground. And we were all aware of the things that were going on because we lived in the town and we could see that many things were happening that we couldn't control, things that were shameful and that were bad. And that the Crisis Staff is being blamed by the police and by the army for a number of those things whereas we, as a body, did not have any de facto influence on those things. And that is why I asked Dr. -- Mr. Kovacevic to put on the agenda the issue of the abolishment of this Crisis Staff. There were other members of the Crisis Staff including Mr. Pavicic and Budimir who thought the same as me, and we were the ones who raised that sometime in mid-June or thereabouts. I can't remember exactly. In any case, in the latter part of June, in the summer, we asked Mr. Kovacevic to do that because Mr. Kovacevic was the president of the Executive Board, and I was its member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what were some of the shameful things that everyone knew were going on in Prijedor that summer?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looting of people's property. During the war operations, there were killings which were not becoming of an organised army and an organised police force. And the fact is that those who were in charge of looking after law and order did not do their job properly. And when I say that, I primarily mean the police. All the time the police was the force that was supposed to protect law and order, unfortunately, the opposite was the case. Private property was plundered, houses, private shops and stores, and everything else. These were the things that were happening and that I call shameful. And I tried to point to those things, and these things were the basis for me to ask for the abolishment of the Crisis Staff, because if the Crisis Staff could not do anything to put the things right, then there was no point for its existence. If it didn't have any mechanisms to introduce order or to issue an order to the police or the army to do so, then the Crisis Staff was pointless, and still it was blamed for many of the things that were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you know about more specific crimes than those you mentioned, don't you, when you say that there was looting and killing and war operations? Can you talk about some of the specific crimes that you knew were going on in Prijedor that summer?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in Banja Luka, I told you that I knew about Keraterm and about the killings of a number of people because the apartment where I resided, that was very close to that Keraterm. It was some 300 or 400 metres away. And in the morning I would hear shooting, and on the following day I would hear from my neighbours that somebody tried to escape from the camp, and then that the army or whoever provided security - the army or the police - committed killings. And I also told you that I had heard of the crime that had happened during one of the transports towards Central Bosnia on Mount Vlasic. I knew of that incident, but I was provided with most of the details much later on. And I also read about the details in the independent newspapers that published the details of those things some three or four years ago. I don't remember exactly. But in any case, I learned some 20 days later after the incidents that had taken place during that transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you think you were one of the few people that knew about these incidents, or were these public knowledge in Prijedor? And I'm talking specifically about the Keraterm massacre and the Vlasic massacre.

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the majority of citizens of Prijedor knew that -- knew about what was going on in Keraterm. And as for Mount Vlasic, I don't know how many people knew about that. But I'm sure that quite a number of people knew about that as well. I learned some 20 days after the incident, and I learned it on the grapevine. It didn't come to me as official information from any of the officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many people did you know personally in the Omarska and Keraterm camps who were detained in Omarska or Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told this Trial Chamber already that I'm not a native of Prijedor, and that I knew very few people of non-Serb ethnicity. The majority of the people I knew were from Zitopromet, the company that I worked for. And luckily for them, quite a number of the people that I knew did not end up in any of these reception centres or prisons or camps. So I can't say that I have a wide circle of acquaintances. I only knew those people that I worked with in the company in which I worked up to the year 1991. One of them was the head of sales. I said that I was the head accountant and the head of the finances. The head of sales was Ahmed Seric. I know to this very day where he is. He is currently residing in Germany. There was another person who was the head of legal affairs, Muharem Harambasic. He also left Prijedor, but currently -- and resided in Norway where he died. After the war, Mr. Anton Bagaric, he stayed in Prijedor. He was the -- a financial operative. And as for other people, I really don't know. I don't know anything about any of them. So these were the people who I knew personally and with whom I socialised at one point or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, it was common knowledge that the Omarska and Keraterm camps existed, and that thousands of people from Prijedor, including very prominent people, were detained in those facilities in 1992. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, you heard that. You knew that in 1992 when it was going on, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that a number of people were taken there, but I didn't know on what grounds. I only knew it as a citizen of Prijedor, and that is what I also told you in my interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Including people like the president of the municipality, the -- Professor Cehajic, the leader of the HDZ party, doctors, directors of companies. These people were known to be interned in the camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know these people personally. It was only later on that I found out that these people had been detained. But I don't know when they were detained. I can't tell you exactly when they went to those centres. But during those days, I didn't know it because I didn't know these people personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that these camps where thousands of people were being held were not discussed in the meetings of the Crisis Staff or the National Defence Council that you attended?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've said is that you could never propose those issues for discussions at the sessions of those bodies. And that was one of the reasons for which I asked for the abolishment of this body because to my mind, if these issues could not be discussed because they did not fall under the authority of this body, of this organ, then I didn't see the point of -- for its existence. Because every time we wanted to discuss plunder, killings, and other such things, they would tell us that this was not our -- within our competence because there are other bodies who were in charge of that. This was not within the competence of any of the municipal organs, and that's why we couldn't put any of these issues on the agenda. But I've told you that personally as a human being, I wanted to learn more in order to take some measures. But we could never raise those issues, and we could never get proper answers to any of the issues that we may have wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My question, sir, is not what you wanted to raise. Let me try to repeat it and make sure I understand your answer. The question is just: Were the Omarska and Keraterm camps discussed in the meetings you attended of the Crisis Staff and National Defence Council or the Executive Board? Any meetings that you attended.

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What was going on in these camps or centres was never discussed. And on the agenda of any of our meetings, we never put any of the things that were going on in any of these centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who set the agenda for the National Defence Council, the Crisis Staff, and the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agenda of the national defence council was set, I suppose, by its president, together with technical services. As for the Crisis Staff, the agenda was set at the sessions of the Crisis Staff. It was proposed by the president, and supplemented by any of the members who felt that something else should be added to the agenda. As for the sessions of the Municipal Assembly, they were chaired by the president of the Municipal Assembly and he was the one who proposed the agenda which was established in advance. So that body was the only one that had its agendas given to it in advance. And those agendas were proposed by the president of the Municipal Assembly. However, even though the agendas were set in advance, every secretary of every secretariat could propose additional issues to be put on the agenda for discussion at the session of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I could either do a few more questions or break now. It's up to Your Honour. Break now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 6.00 precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm so sorry to interrupt the session. I wonder if you would just give me two minutes to raise the matter of timetabling and one other matter. I appreciate Judge Schomburg is not here, and this is on the basis that I raise it before Your Honours and it can be communicated to Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, of course, it is an important reason that Judge Schomburg is not in the courtroom, but there is another important reason. Given that we are sitting under Rule 15 bis in the interest of justice, in order to finish the testimony of those witnesses who are currently in The Hague and who have been waiting for some time to testify in this case, and it is a very expensive procedure, the Chamber will only grant you an audience when the witnesses who are in The Hague have completed the testimony. Of course, it is always open to the OTP to file a written motion on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I promise you, it doesn't require a written motion, and it will take one minute. So we won't waste any time. But I think it's important that Your Honours become aware of something now which then can be communicated to Judge Schomburg immediately -- not immediately, but overnight, so it can be dealt with tomorrow. That's all I'm asking, one minute. It shouldn't require a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I ask if we could go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Koumjian, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Travar, in going to the meetings of the Crisis Staff, I would like to read to you part of the summons interview on page 29, line 16. You were asked by Mr. Malik: "And who would take the notes? Who would take the minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting when you would have discussions?" And you answered: "There was a secretary. There were two people. One of them was the secretary of the assembly who used to take the minutes. And there was also one person from the Ministry of Defence. I can't recall his name, but he was grey-haired, and he had -- he wore glasses. He very often used to take notes, minutes." Sir, would it be correct that those two individuals who took minutes were Mr. Baltic and Spiro Marmat?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess, because, of course, after that statement, I talked with colleagues, and I said that I thought that Mr. Baltic attended Crisis Staff meetings. And Spiro Marmat, obviously I see from this record that he was the one who chaired meetings for the Council for National Defence. So I think it is those two individuals. But at that moment, I couldn't really say because I said that I didn't know about the meetings of this council, but I thought also that Mr. Marmat was present at the Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In my earlier questions, I asked you about Omarska and Keraterm. To be complete, did you discuss the Trnopolje camp at the Crisis Staff meetings, or the meetings of the National Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I didn't discuss it with anyone. Understand by my earlier answer that about these things you couldn't really talk with anyone -- except that perhaps informally with my colleagues in the Crisis Staff, I tried to find out about things that were going on in those centres. But officially at the Crisis Staff meetings, these matters were not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff or the National Defence Council organise convoys from the Trnopolje camp to take people out of Prijedor, such as the convoy on the 21st of August where the massacre occurred that you mentioned? Did they organise any convoys from Trnopolje, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to my knowledge, no. The Crisis Staff and the council -- did you say the Council for National Defence, that they organised it? No. As far as I know, they didn't. Again, once again, I do not know much about the national -- about the Council for National Defence. I don't know what its purpose or its role. I do not know how many times they met. These minutes show that I was present at the meetings, but I don't know what kind of a body it was. And the Crisis Staff didn't organise it, and I don't think that the Council for National Defence did it either because it was not discussed at the meetings that I was present at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff fund Autotransport Prijedor, pay them, for taking people out of the municipality or for taking people to camps?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did not pay that activity or the secretariat. But Autotransport did, like many other companies, turn to us with applications to have certain outlays compensated. So yes, I already said that, Zitopromet, Autotransport, Velepromet, and many other organisations requested that they be reimbursed for whatever expenses, or whatever the army and the police had taken from them and failed to pay for. So perhaps there was some expenditure that was covered for Autotransport, but I do not remember that there was any such outlay paid by the staff for that particular purpose. As a matter of fact, I put it to you that it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, before you is S90. That was the meeting of the National Defence Council on the 29th of September, 1992. Looking at item number 2, if you could just read along with me, item number 2, do you understand that item to be a report on the forthcoming activities regarding the open Trnopolje reception centre? "After a discussion, the following was concluded: "The National Defence Council will take on all the essential obligations regarding the unhindered" -- that's translated as -- "arrival of all persons from the open Trnopolje reception centre according to a list agreed by the municipal Red Cross and the International Red Cross. "2. The public security station in Prijedor will provide escort for the convoy, and the secretariat for the economy and social services will provide vehicles and fuel." Sir, when this item refers to the secretariat for economy and social services, would that be -- would you have been the head of that body at that time, the 29th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this, by the way, 29th of September, would have after the visit of the foreign journalists to Prijedor and the publication of pictures from the Omarska and Trnopolje camps in the international press. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it here. I really cannot remember. Even though I see that a discussion about this took place, all I can do is comment on this. And again, I say I had nothing to do with the Council for National Defence. It says that I was present at the meeting. It says up here. But I cannot. The secretariat for economy was responsible for -- to provide vehicle -- means of transportation and fuel. This could mean, I repeat, these organisations were filing many applications because the army and the police were requisitioning various things, and these organisations were seeking compensation. So I suppose here, it's fuel. So that later on, in some normal period of time, transport in the town could be provided. But I don't remember this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember discussing in any of the bodies in which you were a member the visit of the foreign journalists to Prijedor, the one where they went to the Omarska and Trnopolje camps and published photographs of detainees at those camps?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember those photographs which were carried by media. But I do not remember when this delegation visited the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. My question is: Did you ever discuss that visit either before or afterwards? Either before the visit or afterwards, did you discuss the effect of that international publicity in the Crisis Staff, the National Defence Council, or any other body that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Crisis Staff, but I had no opportunity to discuss this topic in the Crisis Staff. And I wasn't a member of the council except that I did attend the meeting. I mean, I saw it from the minutes, even though I didn't at all know what was the job, what was the field of operation of that body. I've already said that earlier. I do not remember us ever discussing the visit of the International Red Cross. I cannot recall at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that Autotransport Prijedor was not used to take people to the camps or to -- excuse me. I believe I understood you to say that you did not reimburse -- or the Crisis Staff or Executive Board did not reimburse Autotransport Prijedor for taking people to the camps or transporting people out of Prijedor to Croatia or the territory controlled by the Bosniak army. But did the Crisis Staff have any other use of Autotransport Prijedor? Did you use their services for anything else that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember ever ordering for anything except there was frequently the problem of transport; that is, the normal functioning of the town or interurban transport. And Autotransport, because many of its buses had been taken by the army and the police, they simply could not meet the demand. They were simply short of the buses. And those buses that they had at their disposal, often they didn't have the fuel for them. Because I've already said earlier that possibly on the basis of the contract, both the army and the police used their services or used their fuel stocks. And then they asked the Autotransport to give them diesel for buses, and Zitopromet for the bread that they delivered, and Velepromet for other foodstuffs that the army requisitioned because their higher instances, that is, the ministries which funded them or from military reserves, because they did not pay for those, they frequently came to the municipal authorities to have reimbursed the expenses of the army or the police, or sought our help so that together we perhaps -- we could try to get the money for what the army and the police owe them. I believe there was a military army accounting centre existed in the army which paid for all the expenditures of the army. And for the public security station, that is, for police, it was at the ministry or the centre of public security. So I do not exclude the possibility that Autotransport and other organisations sought to have the expenses reimbursed, I mean the expenses of the army and the police, because they could not regularly perform their job. And since they had no access to those who owed them, that is, those who are financing the army, the military accounting centre at the corps level, the Ministry of Defence, that is, budget, then they came to the municipality seeking -- that is, the municipality reimbursed part of the expenses or that we go together and try to collect the money for the services that they had provided. And that is why it would happen that there were certain applications made to the municipality for the reimbursement or the budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S63, and at the same time perhaps S77.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified also earlier, yesterday or today, that the Crisis Staff and your secretariat did not pay the police or army, that they had their own means of payment. Is that correct? Pay salaries.

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the army and the police were under the authority of the republican budget when it came to financing. In other words, that they couldn't be funded from the municipality budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, did you pay part of the salaries for the police from the municipal budget, or the army?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. If you have a document based on which you -- one could conclude that, I would like to see it. There were different applications for assistance and for payments from the budget. But if I may have a document, then maybe I could comment on such a document and explain any of the outlays that may have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll do that. First let's look at S63, which is a document dealing with Autotransport Prijedor. If the English could be put on the ELMO, do you see this, sir, as a document -- first of all, it appears to be authored by the municipal secretariat for the economy, the department for the budget and finance, which I believe you testified was one of four branches of your secretariat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And the subject of this document is: "Autotransport's request for reimbursement of the cost of using buses for the needs of the Crisis Staff in July 1992." Would it be correct that you're talking -- or this document, do you understand it as referring to the Crisis Staff of which you were a member, the one headed by Milomir Stakic in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I read this document, that's what I could understand. But I see this piece of paper for the first time. Let me just tell you that it was possible that some of the materiel -- I am not denying that this department for budget and finances was one part of my secretariat. They could grant reimbursement of some company's expenses if there were funds in the budget. Here, I can see that this was proposed, and that it was sent to the Executive Board of the Prijedor Municipality. But my only comment would be -- is that I really don't know whether it was the Crisis Staff who commissioned any services from Autotransport. Not to my knowledge, it didn't. But it is possible that this proposal was sent in order to help Autotransport to cover for some of their expenses or for Autotransport to be able to meet the demands for running public transportation, local transportation in Prijedor. Again, I say this is the first time I see this document. I didn't see it before. I can't remember it. I'm not denying that this was drafted by one of my departments. I can only comment on this document as the desire of this secretary or secretariat or my department for budget and finances to help Autotransport to cover some of the expenses that it had as an attempt to enable Autotransport to provide its regular services of transporting passengers in Prijedor. I really don't know whether there was the Crisis Staff requirement for any buses. There were no such orders or requirements to my knowledge, and that is all I can say about this document. And I really don't know what kind of expenses would be reimbursed by this, but I'm not denying that this proposal was drafted by one of my departments. And as for the decision being approved and taken by the Executive Board, I don't know. I really don't know what happened with this document and whether this sum of money has ever been paid to the Autotransport as stated herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, reading the first two sentences, it says: "Prijedor ATP has sent an invoice for reimbursement of the cost of using buses for the needs of the Crisis Staff in July 1992." They enclosed records on the transport provided for the needs of the army, the Crisis Staff, and the police." Isn't it quite clear that they're not talking about normal public transportation in this document?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean to say that this was reimbursement of costs for public transportation. I just said that we had a number of applications arriving at our address from different companies, not only Autotransport, but also Velepromet and Zitopromet most often. And that the Executive Board, that is, the department for budget and finances, if there was room to meet these requests, they would meet these requests in order to help these companies to perform their everyday work. It does say here that they did provide some services to the army, the police, and the Crisis Staff. However, who issued the order for the performance of these services, I don't know. I don't know whether there were any grounds for such an invoice to be made. One thing is sure: It was not within the municipal competency to pay any company for the services provided to the army and the police. They did not have to pay those services from the budget. I would really be curious to see what happened with this request for reimbursement, whether any decision was ever taken to that effect by the Executive Board and whether this decision, if made, was implemented. I don't remember this particular application. There were a number of such applications, so I really don't know whether I ever saw this particular application. There were a number of applications, some of which were approved, some of which were rejected. Some of the companies were reimbursed and paid in order to help them to provide their everyday work. What I'm saying is: I don't know whether there was any order by the Crisis Staff to engage the services of Autotransport for something that the auto -- that the Crisis Staff had to do. I don't know whether there is any document proving that services were indeed requested by the Crisis Staff from this company, from Autotransport. If there is a document proving that the Crisis Staff ordered Autotransport to provide them with their services, then I could comment on that because once again I'm saying different applications and requests came to the secretariat for funding from the budget. And those were usually requests for the reimbursement of these companies that had provided services to different institutions or to the police or to the army. Maybe it was somebody who acted on behalf of the Crisis Staff and said, "I would like to order these services or other services." In any case, when we were under obligation to reimburse such services, if the services were provided to a municipal body, then if there were funds in the budget, we would reimburse such a company for the expenses that the municipal body incurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, one of the witnesses who testified for the Defence in this case talked about an operation in July in the Brdo region where Autotransport buses took all of the men from Brdo to the Omarska camp, and then when that was full, to Trnopolje. Were you aware of the use of Autotransport buses in July for this operation?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I don't know what you mean when you say "Brdo." Which part of the area is that? Are you referring to the area around Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Rizvanovici, Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I remember it well, together with Mr. Savanovic, I was in Belgrade. I was away on business. I was not in Prijedor at the time when this incident in Rizvanovici happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, why were you in Belgrade in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1992, the corridor was opened towards Serbia, that is, towards Yugoslavia. So I went there to fetch my sister who was a refugee from Sarajevo. She took the last plane out of Sarajevo in May, and she managed to reach Belgrade. And she was there staying with some distant relatives of ours. I went to fetch her and bring her to Prijedor from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness can now be shown S77.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, S77 is a document dated the 16th of June, 1992. On the bottom, it appears: "President of the Crisis Staff, Milomir Stakic" signature and stamp. And you see in this document entitled "Conclusion," referring to a session held that day, the 16th of June, in the first point it indicates, "Simo Drljaca, Ranko Travar, and Radovan Rajlic are charged with making a comprehensive review of the possibilities and set criteria and recommend to the Crisis Staff the manner of payment to and catering for the army and police in the Prijedor municipality area." Do you recall being assigned this task?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have answered this question already. I can't remember this specific conclusion and this specific task. But I have already said that the problems piled up in our relations with the army and police in terms of their supply with food. So what do we have here? Payment of and catering for the army and police? So the manner of payment and the obligations that -- the commitments that they had for taking food and other stuff from companies. I was assigned the duty, and I believe that this is exactly what this conclusion means, I was assigned with the task to find the possibilities to compensate those companies for the outlays that they had towards the army and the police. And as for the payment of salaries, I believe that this implies the reserve police and the army, that is, those people who were mobilised by the army and the police and who were not professional soldiers and as such were not paid by the army. Their companies, the companies that they worked for, were not in the position to pay their salaries regularly. And I was assigned the task to try and help the families of those people who were mobilised and who no longer received salaries from their companies. It was my task to find ways of finding the manner of paying them, either through their companies or through some other ways. I can't remember this document. I don't know whether I ever received it. But in any case, this was something -- a task that I was assigned with, and I don't remember this commission ever meeting in this composition to discuss this issue. But in any case, at the meetings of the Crisis Staff and in my contacts with the competent bodies of the police and the army, I always tried to find a way to compensate the companies who were in turn paying people who had been mobilised by the army and the police. I'm talking about those who were not professionally engaged by either the police or the army. And thus, they could not receive their monthly salaries from the police and the army. Still, these people had to be paid, these people who were mobilised from various companies. They were entitled to receive salaries either from their companies or they were entitled to receive some compensation from the municipal budget. These people did not have any other source of income, neither them nor their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So, sir, if you could answer this question just yes or no, did you, your secretariat, pay the salaries of the reserve police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether there were any such payments. If there had been, I believe that they were compensations paid to the families of those people. I really can't remember if there is a decision to that effect, I can comment upon it. There may be -- may have been such instances. But the budget was what it was, and I believe that in most cases, we solved the problem by their companies taking loans from commercial banks, and then paying salaries to these people. In more specific terms, I can't remember whether there were any payments to the reserve police or the army. I can't remember. I'm sure that there are documents held by the Ministry of Defence and the police that will show whether there were any such payments. But the whole point of this activity and the task that I was given by the Crisis Staff was to resolve the problem of the payment and the catering for the army and for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the reserve police were among those who were the guards at Omarska and Keraterm and were involved in combat activities committing what you called some shameful deeds in Prijedor in 1992? Weren't many of these members of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mobilised soldiers, just like I was a member of the army in 1991 when I responded to the mobilisation call. When these people were mobilised, they were under the authority of the army, but they were not its professional members. They were not employed by the army. They had to carry out tasks, but they were not professionally engaged. They were mobilised and placed under the command of either the police or the army, depending on whose reserve force they were on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S181, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, while that's -- while that's being prepared, if I could perhaps switch topics and ask you a couple quick questions: Did Pero Colic attend meetings of the Crisis Staff, the commander of the Kozarac Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RANKO TRAVAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He occasionally came to the municipality, just like all the other army representatives. But not often. Whether he attended any of the sessions, I don't know. I know that Mr. Arsic and Mr. Zeljaja attended those sessions, but I can't remember whether Pero Colic was one of the participants also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. On --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown an English page 34, it would be item number 400. On the B/C/S, I could try to help you find the page. In the B/C/S version, I believe would be -- the page with the ERN number ending in 734.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this Section 15, this document S181 is from the Official Gazette of Prijedor. And in appearing in that Gazette is the budget for the Prijedor Municipality. On item 400, it is part of Section -- excuse me, I gave you the wrong item number. Yes, excuse me. Section 15 -- I see there are several 400s, so I apologise. Section 15 of that, which would be on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In English, it's on page 34. I'm not sure -- Section 15 is entitled "Public security station." Do you have that page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If Mr. Lukic could help me, I'd be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We really cannot find, under 15, it says here: [Interpretation] "The municipal board of the party of private initiative."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, I'm referring to Section 15. You'll see the budget is divided into expenditures -- into sections, Section 10 is municipal court; Section 12, public attorney; Section 15, public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How much time do you need to finalise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could finish with this question on this section and come back to the document. I'll finish in a minute, Your Honour. Or actually, perhaps we can come back tomorrow, because the answer may take longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two small issues to address to the parties. Mr. Koumjian, I understand that you tendered the document ERN number P00540818?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And that was 65 ter number 235. Yes, we do tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Objections on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do object, Your Honour, on the basis of authenticity. It's not signed. It's not stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There is a stamp. We have the original -- or the best-evidence copy in Court. This is not a copy, but we could get a colour copy made. But I would like to have that shown to the Defence and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a visible stamp. But still we do object because none of these purported signees are not signed on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Following the policy of this Bench, this document is admitted provisionally as S406A/B. Thank you, Mr. Koumjian. And I have a question to the Defence in relation with the statement of Father Milorad Loncar. When this statement was issued? The date of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to have to get back to the Court on that. I understand that the statement was issued or sent to us sometime after the beginning of the week of the 3rd of March, this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How it come that on the upper part of each page, we have the date 10 March, year 2000?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know why it says the year 2000. That might be from my office faxes that to us on the 10th of March. Our office faxed that to us on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It could be that the fax machine date --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It also could be -- I think my learned friend is trying to perhaps help me, is that it might be the date of the fax machine in the Defence counsel room, that it might have to be reset from time to time. And we have no control over that. But it was faxed to me in the Defence counsel room. But again I'll verify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Please do. But when this statement was issued, signed by Father Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It hasn't yet been signed. I spoke to -- personally to Father Loncar well before the 3rd in preparation of that and we were trying to obtain it. He had other duties, and obviously we were in Court during that time period. I was in the United States the weekend immediately prior, so we were trying to coordinate that. So it was immediately sometime on or around the 3rd, but I'll get the answer to that specific question for the Court tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would just point out that the bottom indicates the date of March 11th, 2003, so I think one of the fax machines just did not have the year set correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Koumjian. And one more question. On page 4 of this document, statement, we read that "After the events during the spring of 1992, I met Dr. Stakic in the village of Omarska." But as far as we are aware, at that time, Dr. Stakic hasn't been in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't have the statement in front of me. The only copy I gave --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did give my only copy this morning to the Court officer who promised to give me a copy of it. I haven't received our copy back. I think in the prior paragraph, it's more specific as to where Father Loncar met with Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And he was there I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: -- Because it's confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we will tell you, as you know, that he was at or near there until the 30th of May, 1992. So that might be that general -- but we will clarify it. April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Spring 1992, "After the events during the spring of 1992, I met Dr. Stakic in the village of Omarska."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will obtain a clarification on that. Thank you for pointing it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Yes, do that. I have no more questions to the parties. And Mr. -- no questions, no issues to raise with regard to the witness? Then I have objections and no submissions. Mr. Travar, as we discussed on Friday and Monday, until your testimony here has concluded, you may not contact representatives of either the Defence or the Prosecution. Please be back tomorrow at 2.15 to continue with your evidence in this case. The trial stays adjourned until 2.15 p.m. tomorrow.
